title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Testability Failure
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether deterministic verifier augmentation (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The preregistered primary estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline), tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Executed run (shared_initial_candidate semantics, model_calls_used = 200) produced SAFE = 200/200 for both arms (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). Estimate = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this execution. We publish the preregistered artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of this testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the reserved exploratory budget, and pilot contingency checks) needed to obtain an informative repeat.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→device‑configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises to reduce operator workload in NetOps but risks outages or policy violations when generated changes are incorrect or misordered. A prevalent mitigation pattern is tool‑augmentation: couple an LLM generator to deterministic validators, sandboxed simulators, or constrained executors in a generate–validate–repair pipeline so that proposed changes are checked before execution. Prior work advocates such pipelines and stresses the importance of workflow‑centred, replayable evaluations to quantify safety and operational trade‑offs (surveys and prototypes summarized in Related Work). 

We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) to quantify whether a deterministic verifier reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial prompt clusters. The preregistration fixed the estimand, sampling plan (N=200 tasks), paired analysis procedure and exclusion/missingness rules, and allowed two generation semantics (independent per‑arm draws or shared_initial_candidate). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve hosted model budget. 

Principal scholarly contribution. Because the executed run produced identical per‑pair candidates that were all labeled SAFE by the deterministic validator, the preregistered paired causal test was mechanically non‑informative (a testability failure, not evidence of verifier efficacy). The paper therefore (1) publishes a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts permitting exact replay; (2) provides an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory test was uninformative; and (3) gives concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations for informative repeats (budgeting for independent per‑arm draws, consuming the preregistered exploratory reserve to calibrate adversarial transforms, and pilot contingency checks). The research question as preregistered was: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → optional repair) change the rate of unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts?
sections.related_work:
Surveys and prototype reports document rapid interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, limited remediation) while cautioning that measured gains are task‑dependent and frequently evaluated on curated case sets rather than replayable workflow tests [1,2,3]. Tool‑augmentation and generate–validate–refine architectures are repeatedly proposed and in experimental reports show reductions in explicit constraint violations when the external verifier faithfully encodes domain constraints [4,1]. Work on guardrails, schema‑based tool interfaces, and secure agent orchestration highlights operational trade‑offs: strict validators can lower accepted unsafe proposals but may increase false refusals and operator burden unless the verifier’s coverage and conservatism are well calibrated [5,6]. 

Methodology guidance literature emphasizes reproducible, sandboxed experiments with deterministic task generators, explicit initial and final states, and archived validator traces so runs can be replayed and failure modes inspected. Our study follows these desiderata: we used a deterministic task generator, archived per‑task manifest and validator traces, and preregistered the paired estimand and missingness/exclusion rules. The present work contributes an artifact‑anchored case study that demonstrates how evaluation semantics (shared vs independent generation, repair usage, adversarial calibration) materially determine whether a confirmatory paired estimand can be tested.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand-2026-01-prereg-v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded − baseline) on binary SAFE indicators produced by the deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10000 resamples and bootstrap_seed = 1729. The preregistration specified N=200 unique tasks in a paired design (planned paired episodes = 400) and power assumptions targeting a ≈7 percentage‑point paired reduction with 80% power (assumed baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15%, yielding required n≈174; preregistered N=200 to allow margin). 

Task generation, scope and seeds. A deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to single‑AS multi‑device topologies and limited fields (admin, mtu, vlan). Each task manifest included initial_state, expected_final_state, workflow policies (required_sequence), difficulty metadata, and a generation_seed. The preregistration reserved up to 50 exploratory calibration tasks to tune adversarial transforms prior to confirmatory execution. 

Pipeline comparisons and generation semantics. Baseline: post‑hoc scoring of the LLM candidate (LLM only). Guarded: scoring the same candidate via deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in a sandbox; the guarded arm could optionally invoke a preregistered single repair call but in the confirmatory episodes repair_provider_trace fields are null (no repairs exercised). The preregistration allowed either independent per‑arm generation (two LLM calls per task) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task shared by both arms). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false) to conserve model budget; model_calls_used = 200 vs preregistered potential maximum_model_calls = 400 for independent draws. Model: declared model = gpt-5-mini (as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json). 

Scoring, determinism, and analysis. Validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full_intent_constraint_validation producing deterministic boolean valid flags and structured violation lists. Confirmatory binary outcomes derived from validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Analysis: paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the 2×2 contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Missingness and retry rules (one automatic retry per failed model call) and contamination checks were applied; deterministic reconciliation confirmed no technical failures, exclusions, or nondeterministic verifier behavior in the confirmatory set.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit. The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200, and maximum_model_calls = 400 (preregistered budget for independent per‑arm draws). Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200; cross‑condition cache reuse was not observed. No tasks were excluded or flagged for nondeterminism; deterministic reconciliation checks passed. 

Primary confirmatory outcomes. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory candidate SAFE: baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. The paired contingency counts are n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI is degenerate at [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). These numerical outputs are direct archival analysis artifacts (analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). 

Representative diagnostic traces. Representative per‑task scoring JSONs show identical shared_initial_candidate content across baseline and guarded episodes; validator traces report validation_before/after with violation_count = 0 and valid = true for each confirmed task. repair_provider_trace entries are null across confirmatory scoring JSONs, confirming that no repair-induced discordance occurred. The analysis/missingness_summary documents complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes. The preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) was not consumed prior to confirmatory execution, so no ROC/refusal estimates are available from the confirmatory artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Why the inferential test was uninformative (artifact‑grounded). The inferential degeneracy arises from three archived, interlocking facts: (1) generation semantics — the run executed shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), so exactly one LLM candidate per task was produced and shared by both arms (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/execution_manifest.json); (2) validator outcomes — deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every sampled candidate as valid (analysis/condition_summary.csv showing baseline and guarded success_rate = 1.0); and (3) absence of repairs — repair_provider_trace fields are null in confirmatory scoring JSONs, so the guarded arm did not produce arm‑specific candidate changes. Conjunction of these facts mechanically prevents discordant paired outcomes and therefore renders McNemar’s paired test uninformative for the preregistered causal estimand. This is a testability failure, not evidence that the guarded pipeline is safe in broader contexts.

Design‑level implications and artifact‑supported recommendations. The artifacts make the resource/trade‑off explicit: independent per‑arm generation (required to create arm‑level stochasticity under the current estimand) would have used ≈400 model calls (preregistered maximum_model_calls) versus the executed shared budget of 200 calls (execution/execution_manifest.json). If the goal is a causal paired contrast of validator presence, the confirmatory plan must enable arm‑level variability: either (a) independent per‑arm generation (budget ≈2× model calls), or (b) ensure the guarded arm performs deterministic repairs that produce candidate changes (and archive repair traces for analysis). Practical repeat plan (archive‑grounded): (1) consume the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) to calibrate adversarial transforms until baseline unsafe rate aligns with power assumptions; (2) run a small deterministic pilot holdout to inspect contingency counts and abort the full confirmatory run if pilot shows a ceiling/floor contingency; (3) if budget‑constrained, change the estimand to an absolute baseline unsafe‑rate estimate or to refusal/repair conversion rates (these alternative estimands were preregistered as secondary/exploratory items). All recommended changes are supported by the preregistration content and execution accounting in the archived bundle.

Threats to validity and operational interpretation. Internal validity: the execution was internally consistent and deterministic (no technical failures or exclusions), but the chosen generation semantics eliminated arm‑level stochasticity for this estimand. Construct validity: the binary SAFE label depends on validator coverage; validators that only encode a restricted configuration fragment (here: admin/mtu/vlan) will miss many real‑world failure modes. External validity: tasks were synthetic single‑AS topologies with limited fields; results do not generalize to production multi‑AS, multi‑vendor settings. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate (≈10–15%); that assumption failed here, invalidating the power justification. Operational implication: teams must weigh additional model‑call cost for independent draws and exploratory calibration against the risk of producing untested changes; our artifact bundle quantifies the per‑task cost difference (200 vs 400 calls) and the reserved exploratory budget, enabling concrete budgeting decisions.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt-5-mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be tested in this run. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts permitting exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the exploratory reserve, pilot contingency checks, and explicit repair‑trace instrumentation) to enable informative repeats. The archived execution and analysis artifacts permit deterministic replication of the diagnosis and should be consulted prior to attempting repeats or production extrapolation.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
